title: Container Complexity, Allocators and Memory Characteristics
objectives: Recall the complexity and memory-layout guarantees of the main STL containers from a blank table
Contrast contiguous and node-based containers in allocation count, per-element overhead and cache behaviour
Explain the Allocator concept and std::allocator's role, and attach a minimal custom allocator to a container
Justify container choices for trading components using complexity, memory and latency-predictability arguments
motivation: Complexity tables tell you how an algorithm scales; memory layout decides how fast it actually runs. A map's O(log n) hides 48-byte nodes scattered across the heap, each one its own allocation; a vector's O(n) find hides a cache-friendly linear scan that outruns the tree at realistic sizes. Add allocators - who supplies the memory, and when - and you have the vocabulary to reason about latency, not just big-O, which is the vocabulary trading-system interviews actually test.

rows: O(n) scan; O(log n) if sorted
reallocation kills all; insert/erase from the position
O(n) scan; O(log n) if sorted
end-push: refs survive, iterators may die; middle ops: all die

blocks.md: Two readings of this table. First, the bounds are **guarantees**, not speeds: an O(n) scan over contiguous memory can beat an O(log n) tree walk for the sizes you actually hold, because the scan streams through cache lines while the tree pointer-chases across the heap. Second, amortized entries - vector's back insertion - are paid in bursts: the reallocation stalls exactly when the buffer is full, which in a trading session is the worst possible moment to stall.

blocks.caption: Same O(n), different constants: contiguous data streams through the prefetcher; every node hop risks a cache miss.

blocks.text: Contiguous vs node-based: the real cost is the node

blocks.md: A node container pays per element, forever. On x86-64 with libstdc++, a std::map<int, int> node is roughly 32 bytes of tree machinery (three pointers plus colour and padding) wrapped around the 16-byte pair - call it 48 bytes before allocator overhead, with **one heap allocation per element**. The same million pairs in a vector cost 16 MB in exactly one allocation, and index arithmetic replaces pointer chasing. The tree's premium buys worst-case bounds and stable iterators, not payload.

blocks.title: One million int-to-int entries, measured in bytes
items: Vector: $10^6 \times 16$ bytes = **16 MB**, one contiguous block, sequential layout, one allocation.
Map nodes: $10^6 \times 48$ bytes = **48 MB** before allocator headers, plus a million allocations at construction.
The 32 MB gap is pure structure: tree pointers and per-node allocation overhead buy O(log n) bounds and iterator stability.
unordered_map sits between: a per-node next pointer (roughly 24-32 bytes for this pair) plus a bucket array of about n pointers, another ~8 MB.

blocks.tex: n \text{ nodes} \;\Rightarrow\; n \text{ allocations}, \qquad 1 \text{ vector} \;\Rightarrow\; 1 \text{ allocation}
blocks.caption: Allocation count, not just byte count, is the node container's hidden cost - each allocation is a potential syscall and a latency spike.

blocks.md: Every STL container's full type includes its allocator: std::vector<T, Alloc>. The default, std::allocator<T>, forwards to ::operator new and ::operator delete - the global heap, one call at a time. Because the allocator is part of the type, vector<int, MyAlloc> is a *different type* from vector<int>: pass allocators through template parameters, not through global tricks. What custom allocators buy: arena buffers that free everything at once, pools sized for fixed node types, and instrumentation like the counter below.

blocks.caption: An instrumenting allocator is the cheapest container profiler you can write - and the count proves the reserve's value.

blocks.md: The minimal C++17 allocator is small: a value_type alias plus allocate/deallocate - allocator_traits supplies every other member by default. The snippet's point is the count: reserve(1000) turns 1,000 push_backs into exactly one allocation. Without it, a doubling policy calls allocate eleven times (capacities 1 through 1024) and moves 1,023 elements along the way - work that scales with the data you already hold.

blocks.title: Allocate before the bell
blocks.md: On a latency-sensitive path the goal is zero allocation after initialisation: reserve every buffer, pre-size every unordered_map (reserve plus a tuned max_load_factor), and where node containers are unavoidable, feed them a pool allocator so nodes come from a pre-allocated arena. A single mid-session reallocation of a million-element buffer never shows up in your average latency - it shows up in the 99.9th percentile, where clients notice.

items: **std::allocator** - the default: global heap per call, stateless, no guarantees beyond correctness.
**std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource** (C++17) - bump-pointer arena over a buffer you own; deallocate is a no-op and everything frees when the resource dies.
**Pool / free-list allocators** - fixed-size chunks sized to node containers (map nodes, list nodes); O(1) alloc and free, no fragmentation.
**Instrumenting allocators** - count calls and track high-water marks to find which container actually allocates on your hot path.

blocks.md: The heuristic ladder: append-only or index-ordered data - vector with reserve (fewest allocations, best cache behaviour). Keys that must stay sorted, best-price reads, range sweeps - map. Keyed lookup with no order, robust hashing, huge n, and tolerance for a rare rehash spike - unordered_map, reserved up front. Work at both ends of a timeline - deque. Always need exactly the single best element - priority_queue. And when two options sit in the same big-O class, decide on constants: allocation count, element size, cache behaviour - measured, not assumed.

guidedExercise.prompt: A book holds 250,000 price levels as a std::map<double, int>. Model each node as a 32-byte tree header plus the 16-byte payload (double + int, padded), ignoring allocator slack. (a) How many MB do the map's nodes use in total, and how many allocations does building the map make? (b) The same 250,000 levels in one std::vector<std::pair<double, int>> reserved up front: how many MB, and how many allocations? (c) State the overhead in MB and one concrete benefit the map buys with it.
hints: Node = header + payload, one allocation per node.
Vector cost = element size times count, in one allocation.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Per node $32 + 16 = 48$ bytes, so $250{,}000 \times 48 = 12{,}000{,}000$ bytes = **12 MB**, built through **250,000 allocations**. (b) $250{,}000 \times 16 = 4{,}000{,}000$ bytes = **4 MB** in **one** allocation. (c) Overhead = **8 MB** of tree machinery and allocation granularity - bought for O(log n) worst-case bounds, sorted sweeps in key order, and iterators that never invalidate except on erase.

independentExercise.prompt: Three components, one container decision each, justified by complexity, layout or allocation behaviour: (a) an append-only buffer of up to 5,000 16-byte fills, replayed by index after the close; (b) a price ladder where the engine reads the best level instantly and sweeps levels in order at the close; (c) a symbol-to-position lookup over 8,000 symbols, probed millions of times per session, with no ordering need. For (a), also give the byte count and allocation count after reserve(5000).
hints: Append-only plus indexed replay means contiguous storage.
Ordered sweeps and best-first reads mean a tree; unordered probes with a good hash mean a hash table, reserved up front.
independentExercise.solution: (a) **std::vector<Fill> with reserve(5000)**: $5000 \times 16 = 80{,}000$ bytes, **one** allocation, push_back never reallocates, indexed replay is O(1). (b) **std::map<price, level>**: best price in O(1) via prev(end())/begin(), inserts in O(log n), ordered iteration for the close-out sweep, and a hard worst case. (c) **std::unordered_map** with reserve(8000) and a tuned max_load_factor: average O(1) probes, and reserving up front ensures the table never rehashes mid-session.

commonMistakes: Reading complexity tables as speed tables - a contiguous O(n) scan beats a scattered O(log n) tree walk at realistic sizes; constants and cache dominate.
Forgetting that the allocator is part of the container's type - vector<int, A> and vector<int> are unrelated types that do not interconvert.
Counting only bytes and ignoring allocation count - a million map nodes mean a million allocations, each a potential latency spike.
Reserving only the vector and forgetting unordered_map - reserve() plus max_load_factor prevent mid-session rehashes.
Assuming an allocator changes complexity guarantees - it changes who provides memory and how, not the algorithmic bounds of the container.
realWorldApplication: Capacity planning for production services is this lesson in disguise: buffer pre-sizing, allocator selection and node-vs-contiguous tradeoffs decide whether a service holds p99 latency under load or collapses in allocation spikes.
quantFinanceApplication: Low-latency desks pre-reserve every container and use arena or pool allocators so no allocation syscall lands on the hot path during trading hours - the 99.9th-percentile latency report is where skipped reserves become visible.
summary: Know the map by heart: vector (contiguous, amortized O(1) back), deque (blocks, O(1) ends), list (nodes, O(1) given iterator), map (nodes, O(log n)), unordered_map (nodes + buckets, O(1) average / O(n) worst).
Node containers pay per element: roughly 32 bytes of structure plus one allocation per node; contiguous containers pay once and stream through cache lines.
The allocator is part of a container's type; std::allocator forwards to the global heap, and a minimal custom allocator needs only value_type, allocate and deallocate.
reserve(n) on a vector makes a 1,000-push loop a single allocation; without it, doubling growth allocates eleven times and moves 1,023 elements.
Same big-O class: decide on constants - allocation count, element size, cache behaviour - measured with benchmarks, not assumed.

quiz.prompt: Which container stores all of its elements in one contiguous allocation?
quiz.explanation: The vector's elements live in one buffer. list, map and set are node-based - one heap allocation per element - and unordered containers add a bucket array on top.

reserve(1000) allocates once and guarantees capacity() >= 1000, so none of the 1,000 push_backs reallocates. Without the reserve, doubling growth would call allocate eleven times (capacities 1 through 1024).

quiz.prompt: A std::map<int, int> holds 1,000,000 entries. Model each node as 32 bytes of tree header plus the 16-byte payload, ignoring allocator slack. Compared with a single vector of the same 16-byte pairs, how many extra MB does the map's structure cost?
quiz.explanation: Map: 1,000,000 x 48 bytes = 48 MB. Vector: 1,000,000 x 16 bytes = 16 MB. The 32 MB difference is tree pointers, colour and padding - structure, not payload.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about allocators are true?
options: The allocator is part of a container's type: vector<int, A> differs from vector<int>
std::allocator delegates to global operator new / operator delete
reserve reduces the number of allocations a push loop performs
std::vector cannot be given a custom allocator
quiz.explanation: Alloc is a template parameter, so different allocators mean different types (0). std::allocator is a thin forwarder to the global heap (1). reserve pre-buys capacity so the loop allocates once instead of logarithmically often (2). vector's second template parameter exists precisely to accept custom allocators, so (3) is false.

quiz.prompt: Iterating 1,000,000 int elements is markedly faster over a vector than over a list even though both are O(n). The dominant reason:
options: list iterators are bidirectional, which is slower by definition
vector's contiguous layout streams through cache lines while each list node risks a cache miss
vector's operator[] is O(1) while list traversal is O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: Both traversals are O(n); the constant differs. Contiguous memory lets the hardware prefetcher pull whole cache lines ahead, while pointer-chasing a scattered node per element typically stalls once per node on memory latency.

quiz.prompt: What is a monotonic (arena) allocator and why does it suit the hot path?
quiz.modelAnswer: It hands out memory by bumping a pointer through a pre-allocated buffer and frees everything at once when the arena dies; no per-object deallocation and no allocation syscalls mid-session.
quiz.explanation: C++17 ships it as std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource: allocate is a pointer bump, deallocate is a no-op, and the whole buffer returns when the resource is destroyed - exactly the zero-syscall behaviour a hot path wants.

flashcards.back: The default Allocator: forwards allocate/deallocate to global operator new/delete. The allocator is part of the container's type, and allocator_traits supplies defaults for everything a C++17 allocator may omit.

flashcards.front: CountingAlloc vector: reserve(1000) then 1000 push_backs - allocation count?
flashcards.back: Exactly 1 - reserve(n) allocates at most once and guarantees capacity() >= n, so no push_back reallocates.

Contiguous (vector/array): one allocation, cache-line streaming, O(1) random access - but O(n) insert/erase and reallocation invalidates. Node-based (list/map/unordered): O(1)-given-iterator or O(log n) operations and stable nodes - but 24-48 bytes of structure per element and pointer-chasing cache misses.

flashcards.front: Memory model of a std::map node (x86-64, libstdc++)
flashcards.back: About 32 B of tree header (3 pointers + colour + padding) plus the payload, one heap allocation per element - e.g. map<int,int>: about 48 B/node vs 16 B/element in a vector.
